title: Quantum_artificial_life
summary:
Quantum artificial life is the application of quantum algorithms with the ability to simulate biological behavior. Quantum computers offer many potential improvements to processes performed on classical computers, including machine learning and artificial intelligence. The growing advancement of quantum computers has led researchers to develop quantum algorithms for simulating life processes.

Researchers have designed a quantum algorithm that can accurately simulate Darwinian Evolution. The complete simulation of artificial life on quantum computers was notably implemented by Alvarez-Rodriguez, Sanz, Lomata, and Solano on an IBM quantum computer. Individuals were realized as two qubits, one representing the genotype and the other the phenotype. The genotype is copied to transmit genetic information through generations, and the phenotype depends on genetic information and interactions with the environment.

When two individuals interact, exchanges of information between phenotypes may or may not occur based on their existing values. When both genotypes are alike, no information is exchanged. When the genotypes differ, the phenotypes are exchanged between the two individuals. This procedure produces a constantly changing predator-prey dynamic. Long-living qubits with a larger genetic makeup are at a disadvantage, since information is only exchanged when interacting with individuals of different genetic makeup, giving the short-lived population the advantage.

There are two ways in which the individual can mutate: through random single qubit rotations and by errors in the self-replication process. Due to the no-cloning theorem, it is impossible to produce perfect copies of systems originally in unknown quantum states. However, quantum cloning machines make it possible to create imperfect copies, introducing some degree of error. The presence of mutations is critical for providing randomness and biodiversity. The first experimental realization was on IBM's ibmqx4 cloud quantum computer, encoding behaviors such as self-replication, mutation, interaction between individuals, and death.
